title: The Cache That Didn't Help
summary: Someone added a 64 GB Redis cache to save an overloaded database. The hit ratio is 33% and the DB is still on fire.
scenario: A document service gets 3,000 requests per second, almost all reads. Users open their own documents, so there are no viral hot keys: every read is for a different key.
The database was overloaded, so the team added a big Redis cache. It barely helped. Two-thirds of reads still miss and go to the database.
Make reads reliable and stay within budget. Spending money on things that don't help is a design flaw too.

functional: Let users open their own documents
Read each document by its own key (no shared hot keys)
nonFunctional: Handle 3,000 requests/s, 95% reads with almost no hot keys
Average latency at or below 60 ms
Cost under $900 / month (no spending on things that don't help)

objectives.label: Average latency at or below 60 ms

hints: Run it and look at the cache hit ratio. Why is it so low with 64 GB of memory?
Caches pay off when many requests share a few keys. Here only 5% of reads are hot. You need more database read capacity, and the cache isn't earning its keep.
Adding SQL read replicas while keeping the cache goes over budget. Replace the SQL DB with a NoSQL store with 2 replicas (10,000 rps of reads and writes) and remove the cache.
explanation: Cache effectiveness depends on access skew, not cache size. With a uniform key distribution, the hit ratio is roughly cache size / working set, and a huge working set means a low ratio no matter how much memory you add.
Measure before you cache: if the top 1% of keys don't account for a big share of reads, a cache will mostly add latency on misses and cost.
When reads are spread out, scale the data tier itself: read replicas, or a partitioned store that spreads keys across shards.
Removing components is a valid design move. Every component costs money, adds a failure mode, and needs someone on call for it.
